clue.text: Characteristic of player chasing female

indicators.note: something chasing comes after what it pursues, so the player word is placed behind the female word

parts.note: F is the standard abbreviation for female
a player on the stage is a performer in a play

explanation.surface: A stage performer's defining trait is that he keeps pursuing women.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Player' suggests a womaniser in the surface, which suits the chasing; in the wordplay it is simply a stage performer.
explanation.definitionFit: A factor is an element or contributing feature, so it can stand for a noun meaning a distinguishing feature.

clue.text: Just open a can

parts.note: taken as written
a can and a jar are both containers for keeping food

explanation.surface: Instructions to barely open a tin.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads 'open' as a verb with 'a can' as its object; actually 'Just open' is an adjectival phrase describing a door left slightly apart.
explanation.definitionFit: A door left ajar is open only slightly, barely unclosed, exactly what 'just open' describes.

clue.text: Did Prize with no doubt filling in Tramp

indicators.note: a filling sits inside something else, as jam inside a sandwich, so one word goes within the other

parts.note: to tramp is to walk heavily, to tread; the outer word, split around the filling
being sure means having no doubt

explanation.surface: The setter Tramp confidently claims to have won a prize.
explanation.walkthrough: Tramp is the setter's own pseudonym, so the reader takes it as a name; here it is a verb meaning to walk heavily.
explanation.definitionFit: To treasure something is to prize or cherish it, so 'did prize' is its past tense.

clue.text: Transformed navy dress taken up on the inside

indicators.note: being on the inside places the dress word within the navy word

parts.note: RN is the Royal Navy

indicators.note: in a down clue, taking something up lifts it so it reads from bottom to top, backwards

parts.note: a robe is a long loose garment, a kind of dress

explanation.surface: A sailor's outfit has been altered by taking in the hem.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone reborn has been spiritually renewed, given a fresh start, so they have been fundamentally changed.

clue.text: Argument without coppers

parts.note: ex is Latin for out of, so it can mean without, as in ex dividend
coppers are small low-value coins, i.e. loose change

explanation.surface: A row breaks out with no police around.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coppers' suggests police; in British usage it also means copper-coloured pennies, the small change in your pocket.
explanation.definitionFit: An exchange can be a heated swapping of words, a row or quarrel between two people.

clue.text: Jack, perhaps sets up lines used when changing stories in US?

definitions.text: lines used when changing stories in US?

parts.note: a car jack is one example of a device that raises things
one pitches a tent by setting it up

explanation.surface: Someone called Jack rearranges the plot lines when adapting stories for American audiences.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stories' are floors of a building, spelt that way in the US; changing floors happens in an elevator, the US word for a lift.
explanation.definitionFit: Elevator pitches are brief sales speeches short enough to deliver during one lift ride between floors, hence the lines used then.

clue.text: Husband during affair in contact with escort

indicators.note: something happening during an event falls within its span, so the husband letter sits inside

parts.note: a caper is an escapade or affair
H is the abbreviation for husband
a switch or connection that is on is in contact

explanation.surface: A married man in the middle of an affair keeps in touch with a paid companion.
explanation.definitionFit: A chaperon accompanies a young person to supervise them, an escort in the older protective sense of the word.

clue.text: Copying recording without introduction

indicators.note: having no introduction means the word loses its opening letter

parts.note: taping something is recording it on tape

explanation.surface: Someone is pirating a recording, missing its opening.
explanation.definitionFit: To ape someone is to imitate or mimic them, so aping means imitating.

clue.text: Person with couple in orgy? See Rob aroused

indicators.note: aroused means stirred up, so the letters are stirred into a new order

parts.note: the letters taken as written, punctuation ignored

explanation.surface: A racy invitation to watch Rob get excited at an orgy, with a third wheel tagging along.
explanation.walkthrough: In British slang, playing GOOSEBERRY means being the unwanted third person tagging along with a couple.
explanation.definitionFit: A gooseberry is the awkward extra person present when a romantic pair want to be alone together.

clue.text: Stamped addressed envelope including wrong label is fit to go

indicators.note: including something means holding it inside, so the envelope surrounds the other letters

parts.note: SAE is the British abbreviation for a stamped addressed envelope

indicators.note: something wrong is not in its right order, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A return envelope with a misprinted label is still fine to post.
explanation.definitionFit: Something saleable is in a fit state to be sold, ready to go to a buyer.

clue.text: Friends live lives around work

parts.note: to live is to be; I am means I exist

indicators.note: around means surrounding, so the second word wraps around the work word

parts.note: he lives means he is, he exists
a machine that works goes

explanation.surface: A slogan about friends living their lives around their jobs.
explanation.walkthrough: Live and lives are read as forms of the verb to be, not as living a life.
explanation.definitionFit: Amigos is Spanish for friends, often used jokingly in English for pals or companions.

clue.text: Lying with members out, leader gasped after reorganisation

indicators.note: a reorganisation puts things in a new arrangement, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: the letters taken as written

explanation.surface: A collapsed figure sprawls on the floor while the boss gasps at the restructuring of the party's membership.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Members' looks like party or club members; here it means limbs.
explanation.definitionFit: To be spreadeagled is to lie with arms and legs stretched wide, limbs splayed out.

clue.text: Let too much light in: no more flash

parts.note: something that is over has finished, there is no more of it
to flash is to expose oneself indecently

explanation.surface: A photographer's tip: switch off the flash or the picture will be too bright.
explanation.definitionFit: To overexpose film is to give it excessive light during shooting, washing out the picture.

clue.text: State of party animal off his head?

indicators.note: taking off a head removes the top, so the word loses its first letter

parts.note: a raver is someone who loves wild parties

explanation.surface: A question about the condition of a reveller who is out of his mind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Off his head' reads as drunk or high, apt for a party animal, but it is an instruction to remove his first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To aver is to declare or assert firmly, the verb sense of state.

clue.text: Smelled area out of cage: zoo did badly

indicators.note: doing something badly gets it wrong, so the letters come out jumbled
the word escapes its cage, the outer letters around it, so only its interior survives

parts.note: the inside two letters of the word, with its outer pair removed
the letters taken as written

explanation.surface: An animal escaped from its enclosure because the zoo performed poorly, and the place stank.
explanation.walkthrough: The trap is removing A from CAGE; instead AREA itself sheds its cage of outer letters. ODORIZED is the American spelling.
explanation.definitionFit: To odorize something is to give it a scent, so a thing odorized has been made to smell.

clue.text: False people out to impress

indicators.note: out can mean wrong or off course, so the letters are put in a different order

parts.note: the letters taken as written

explanation.surface: Fake people are only trying to make a good impression.
explanation.definitionFit: Imposters pretend to be someone they are not, deceitful frauds whose identity is a sham.

clue.text: End terrace with a disadvantage

parts.note: Ter is the abbreviation for Terrace in street addresses
a minus is a drawback or disadvantage

explanation.surface: An end-of-terrace house comes with a drawback.
explanation.walkthrough: An end terrace is the British house at the end of a row of joined houses, which tempts solvers to take both words together.
explanation.definitionFit: A terminus is the final stop of a railway or bus line, its end point.

clue.text: Recall from past political party hosting Republican creep

indicators.note: a host has guests inside, so the party word holds the others within it

parts.note: the DUP is the Democratic Unionist Party of Northern Ireland
R is the abbreviation for Republican
to edge is to creep forward gradually

explanation.surface: A party resurrects an old memory when it welcomes an unpleasant Republican.
explanation.walkthrough: Northern Irish unionists and Irish republicans are opponents, which gives the surface its bite; 'creep' is a verb, not an unpleasant person.
explanation.definitionFit: To dredge up an old matter is to bring it back from obscurity, reviving a memory.

clue.text: Fighter trained to drop amateur with sharp blow on the counter

indicators.note: counter means opposite in direction, so the pair is read backwards

parts.note: A is the abbreviation for amateur
a rap is a sharp knock

explanation.surface: A boxer is coached to knock down a novice with a sharp counter-punch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drop' suggests flooring an opponent; for the definition it is a parachute drop.
explanation.definitionFit: A para is a paratrooper, a soldier trained to be dropped by parachute into battle.

clue.text: Barrel placed in bar is full

indicators.note: placed in means put inside, so the barrel word goes within the bar word

parts.note: a rod is a bar of metal or wood
a tun is a large cask for beer or wine

explanation.surface: A keg has been put in the pub, which is now packed.
explanation.definitionFit: Rotund describes a plump round figure, a full or rounded shape, as in a full face.

clue.text: Calls to sex maniac's mobile? About 50

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the rearranged letters go around the number
something mobile moves about, so the letters shift into new positions

parts.note: the letters taken as written
L is the Roman numeral for fifty

explanation.surface: A pervert's mobile phone has received about fifty calls.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mobile' looks like a phone, fitting 'calls', but it is the signal to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Exclamations are sudden cries or shouts, which is what calls mean in the sense of loud utterances.

clue.text: Right to run

definitions.meaning: first meaning: lawful, genuine, above board
second meaning: read as two words, a slang phrase for running away

explanation.walkthrough: Split into two words, the answer becomes the slang phrase LEG IT, meaning to run off fast.
explanation.definitionFit: Legit is short for legitimate, meaning proper and lawful, while leg it is informal slang for fleeing on foot.

clue.text: Pointer from signal over line

indicators.note: over here means covering, so the signal word spreads across and around the line letter

parts.note: a cue is a signal to begin
L is the abbreviation for line

explanation.surface: Guidance taken from a signal on a railway line.
explanation.walkthrough: L goes inside CUE.
explanation.definitionFit: A clue is a hint that points a solver towards an answer, so a pointer in the sense of an indication.

clue.text: Naked kissing leading to head

indicators.note: naked means stripped of its covering, so the word loses its outer letters

parts.note: snogging is British slang for kissing passionately

explanation.surface: A tale of nude kissing that ends up going to someone's head.
explanation.walkthrough: Snog is British slang for a passionate kiss; strip off its first and last letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Noggin is informal slang for a person's head, as in use your noggin.

clue.text: Hold alert insect

parts.note: to house something is to hold or contain it
fly is British slang for sharp or knowing

explanation.surface: An instruction to keep watch for a bug.
explanation.walkthrough: Fly in British slang means streetwise and alert, as in a fly operator.
explanation.definitionFit: The housefly is the common two-winged pest found indoors, a familiar kind of insect.

clue.text: They might form impressions of believers carrying holy books

indicators.note: carrying means holding within, so the believers word wraps around the books

parts.note: deists believe in a creator God without revealed religion
NT is the New Testament, a set of holy books

explanation.surface: Religious believers clutching scripture might make an impression on others.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Impressions' suggests reputation, not moulds of teeth.
explanation.definitionFit: Dental practitioners take moulds of patients' teeth, called impressions, to make crowns and dentures.

clue.text: Daughter remains in tears

parts.note: D is the abbreviation for daughter
ashes are the remains after cremation

explanation.surface: A daughter weeps over her parent's remains.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tears' wants to be crying, but it is the verb meaning rushes.
explanation.definitionFit: To dash is to rush or hurry, and tears in the sense of racing along means the same.
